text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCalculate a mean free path and follow why a heat bath produces Boltzmann factors. 01The distance between interactions If scatterers have uniform number density n and cross section σ, a narrow path of length x encounters an expected nσx targets. Set nσℓ = 1 to find the mean free path. ℓ = 1nσ = 1κρ, τopt = Rℓ = κρR The second expression is the optical depth of a uniform medium. We write τopt to distinguish it from a lifetime. 02Many scatterings make a random walk After N random steps, the net displacement is roughly √N ℓ. Escaping a region of radius R needs N ∼ (R/ℓ)² steps. Each takes ℓ/c, giving the following diffusion-time estimate. A photon’s random walkOne possible path through many scatterings. Pale circles indicate scatterers and dark dots indicate changes of direction. The step lengths vary; their mean is the mean free path. Distinguish total path length from net displacement.View larger diagram ↗ tdiff ∼ R2cℓ (ℓ ≪ R) Scattering alone need not establish a blackbody photon distribution. Thermalization also needs processes such as sufficient absorption and emission. Dilute gas may not be in local thermodynamic equilibrium. 03An isolated whole, with a subsystem exchanging heat For an isolated “small system + large heat bath,” count the microstates at fixed total energy equally: the microcanonical starting point. The probability that the small system has energy Eᵢ is proportional to the bath’s number of states at Etot − Eᵢ. S = kB ln Ω, ΔSbath ≈ −EiT We use the thermodynamic relation that a large bath losing energy Eᵢ loses approximately Eᵢ/T of entropy while its temperature stays nearly fixed. Divide by kB and exponentiate to obtain the ratio of state counts. pi ∝ gi exp(−EikBT) gᵢ counts states with the same energy: their statistical weight. This is the canonical distribution of the subsystem. 04For two levels, simply take a ratio n2n1 = g2g1exp(−E2−E1kBT) For a 10.2 eV separation at 10⁴ K, kBT ≈ 0.862 eV, giving exp(−11.8) ≈ 7.2 × 10⁻⁶. Thermal excitation is scarce. The overall ionization fraction requires a separate calculation. Extension: entropy maximization with multipliers α and β This optional part uses derivatives, but no differential equations. For classical independent particles with populations nᵢ, Ω = N! ∏gᵢⁿⁱ/nᵢ!. At large populations use Stirling’s approximation: ln n! ≈ n ln n − n. F = ln Ω − α(Σni−N) − β(ΣniEi−U) Maximize lnΩ while keeping Σnᵢ = N and ΣnᵢEᵢ = U fixed. Differentiating with respect to each nᵢ gives −ln(nᵢ/gᵢ) − α − βEᵢ = 0. Exponentiate to solve. ni = gie−αe−βEi, β = 1kBT Identifying β uses the thermodynamic entropy–temperature relation; α normalizes particle number. Applying this classical counting directly to photons does not yield Planck’s law: photons are bosons with nonconserved number. The next chapter uses Einstein coefficients instead. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. What happens to the mean free path when the scatterer density doubles? Show the answer and reasoning It halves: ℓ = 1/(nσ), assuming the interaction cross section remains unchanged.
